title: Measles Is Becoming So Common That Treatments May Soon Be Needed
gist: As US measles cases in 2026 have already surpassed all of 2025's total by July amid declining vaccination rates, a small group of biotech firms and academic labs (Invivyd, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Vanderbilt/Saravir Biopharma, Georgia State University) are racing to develop monoclonal antibody and antiviral treatments, but weak pharma economics and rising anti-vaccine sentiment threaten both funding and real-world adoption.

insights.claim: US measles cases in 2026 had already surpassed 2025's full-year total of 2,289 by July, up from just 285 cases in all of 2024, driven by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude year-over-year case surge signals an accelerating public health crisis and a fast-growing addressable market for measles-specific therapeutics.
insights.quote: the US had already surpassed last year’s 2,289 measles cases, and it’s only July. For comparison, there were just 285 cases in all of 2024.
insights.locator: Fueled by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah

insights.claim: Measles requires at least 95 percent two-dose community vaccination coverage to protect immunocompromised people and infants under 12 months, but vaccination rates have dipped well below that threshold in many parts of the US.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A hard herd-immunity threshold being breached in multiple regions explains why outbreaks are compounding rather than staying isolated.
insights.quote: at least 95 percent of people in a community need to receive both doses of the measles vaccine to protect immunocompromised individuals and infants under 12 months old

themes.theme: Why Treatments Are Only Now Emerging

insights.claim: Because measles vaccination was historically so effective, there was little medical or financial incentive to develop dedicated measles treatments; only the recent resurgence in cases has pushed biotech companies and academic groups to begin treatment work, with products likely still years from availability.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: This is an emerging, previously nonexistent therapeutic category being created in real time by a public health failure — early-stage biotech names entering it are worth tracking before the market matures.
insights.locator: Up until recently, measles vaccination has been so effective

insights.claim: Invivyd, a Connecticut biotech that previously developed a Covid monoclonal antibody, is developing a monoclonal antibody for measles administered via IV or injection that mimics natural immune antibodies and could provide short-term protection lasting up to a few months during an outbreak.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Invivyd is a named, identifiable biotech actor positioning to be first-mover in measles post-exposure prophylaxis, leveraging its existing Covid mAb manufacturing know-how.
insights.quote: What we’re seeing now as we get a resurgence of measles in communities is a horrible lack of options when somebody gets exposed
insights.locator: says Michael Mina, an epidemiologist and chief medical officer of Invivyd

insights.claim: Invivyd has not yet tested its measles antibody in humans and is still compiling the data needed for the FDA to authorize clinical trials, even as health care providers are already asking when the therapy will be available.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Pre-clinical stage means a multi-year runway before any product launch; watch for FDA clinical-trial clearance as the first concrete catalyst.
insights.locator: Invivyd, which developed a monoclonal antibody for Covid

insights.claim: Researchers at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, led by president and CEO Erica Ollmann Saphire, published a study in May 2026 identifying human antibodies that block measles infection by binding key viral sites; an infusion of these antibodies produced a 500-fold lower viral load in rodents.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified pre-clinical efficacy result (500x viral load reduction) gives an early benchmark for how potent measles antibody candidates could be.
insights.quote: An infusion of these antibodies resulted in a 500-fold lower viral load in rodents.
insights.locator: In May, Saphire and her team published a study

insights.claim: Saphire argues that a preventive or treatment tool for measles is still cheaper than managing an outbreak or a fatal case of encephalitis in a child, making the economic case for funding measles antibody research despite thin standalone drug-market economics.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Frames measles treatment R&D as a public-health cost-avoidance investment rather than a standalone pharma profit play, which matters for how funders and governments should evaluate ROI.
insights.quote: A tool by which you could prevent or treat disease is still cheaper than managing an outbreak or managing a case of fatal encephalitis in a child.
insights.locator: I think this is a real opportunity to solve a public health problem

insights.claim: The monoclonal antibody combination that became Evusheld, the Covid treatment, was created in just 25 days by Vanderbilt University scientists; that same group has since discovered potent measles antibodies and partnered with small biotech firm Saravir Biopharma to continue development.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Vanderbilt's demonstrated ability to produce a viable antibody combination in 25 days for Covid suggests measles antibody development could move unusually fast if funded; Saravir Biopharma is a small-cap name to watch.
insights.locator: The monoclonal antibody combination that became Evusheld

insights.claim: James Crowe of the Vanderbilt Center for Antibody Therapeutics says the strategy is to combine two monoclonal antibodies to drastically cut the chance the measles virus mutates to evade treatment, and believes the antibodies isolated so far are potent enough to be formulated as a single long-acting shot.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A single long-acting-shot product profile, if realized, would be far more commercially attractive and easier to distribute than repeat IV dosing — a key product-design detail to monitor.
insights.quote: The antibodies that we have isolated are so potent, they strongly inhibit the virus. We feel for sure they could be formulated as a single, long acting shot
insights.locator: James Crowe, an immunologist and director of the Vanderbilt Center for Antibody Therapeutics

insights.claim: Researchers at Georgia State University identified an oral antiviral drug and tested it in rats, ferrets, and dogs infected with related orthoparamyxovirus subfamily viruses (since these animals can't contract human measles); the drug lowered viral load and all treated animals survived, but it has not yet been tested in people.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: An oral antiviral candidate, if it advances, could be cheaper and more scalable than IV/injectable monoclonal antibodies, but it remains at an early animal-model stage with no human data yet.
insights.locator: Researchers at Georgia State University identified an oral antiviral drug

insights.claim: Antivirals for measles face a structural limitation: they tend to be short-lived and must usually be given very soon after infection or symptom onset to work, and drugs toxic enough to kill the virus often carry significant side effects for patients.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Narrow timing windows and toxicity tradeoffs likely limit antivirals to a niche use case relative to monoclonal antibodies, which can be given for broader post-exposure prophylaxis.
insights.locator: Antivirals could also be used as a strategy to treat measles

insights.claim: In early 2022 the US government spent $855 million for 1.7 million doses of Evusheld, the Covid monoclonal antibody; the drug itself was free to patients, but some faced hundreds of dollars in out-of-pocket administration costs, illustrating the cost structure a future measles monoclonal antibody could carry.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: This is a concrete government-spend and patient-cost benchmark (~$500/dose federal outlay plus consumer administration fees) for pricing and stockpiling analysis of a future measles monoclonal antibody.
insights.locator: Monoclonal antibodies could also be costly for patients and insurers

insights.claim: Manufacturing monoclonal antibodies at scale is costly and complex, and clinical trials cost millions of dollars, typically requiring pharmaceutical partners for funding; but drugs for infectious diseases are generally not big money-makers due to the sporadic nature of outbreaks and short treatment courses, making measles treatments a hard commercial sell for pharma companies.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: The core bottleneck for this emerging category is financing, not science — investors should watch for pharma partnership or government contract announcements as the key leading indicator of progress.
insights.locator: A key step toward getting these treatments into human trials

insights.claim: Once measles monoclonal antibodies are ready for human testing, regulators will need to determine trial design, since new drugs are typically tested in adults first for safety even though measles complications are more likely to hospitalize unvaccinated children.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A mismatch between the standard adult-first trial pathway and the pediatric population most at risk could add regulatory friction and delay to market entry.
insights.locator: Once these monoclonal antibodies are ready for human testing

insights.claim: Some disease models predict measles could become endemic in the US within the next 25 years even at current state-level vaccination rates.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A 25-year endemic-disease trajectory implies a durable, structurally growing long-term market for measles treatments rather than a transient outbreak-driven blip.
insights.locator: Some disease models predict that measles could become endemic

insights.claim: James Crowe predicts there will be hundreds of thousands of measles cases and resulting deaths if current trends continue, and argues there is urgency to finish funding and completing measles treatment research now.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A stark casualty forecast from a leading antibody researcher is a potential catalyst for accelerated public and private funding of measles therapeutics.
insights.quote: I think there’s going to be hundreds of thousands of cases,” he says. “People are going to die. There’s some urgency to finishing this work.
insights.locator: Crowe says it's important that work on measles treatments gets funded

insights.claim: During the Utah measles outbreak, some parents refused to let doctors give their children immune globulin, a broad antibody mixture derived from donated plasma, showing that anti-vaccine sentiment can extend to rejecting other antibody-based treatments too.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: This is direct evidence that vaccine-hesitant demand may not simply convert into treatment demand, undercutting the addressable market thesis for new measles therapeutics.
insights.locator: But during the Utah measles outbreak

insights.claim: Anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. leading the US Department of Health and Human Services, where he has cast doubt on vaccines, depression treatments, and other established medical treatments, adding a policy-level headwind to adoption of new measles therapeutics.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
entities: Department of Health and Human Services
insights.so_what: A skeptical HHS leadership is a top-down political risk factor that could slow endorsement, funding, or uptake of new measles treatments regardless of their clinical merit.
insights.locator: anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream

insights.claim: Michael Mina of Invivyd hopes people who have refused vaccines will still be open to a monoclonal antibody because it can be framed as a molecule the body creates naturally, rather than as a vaccine.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Framing/marketing as a 'natural' antibody rather than a vaccine could be a deliberate adoption strategy to bypass vaccine hesitancy, though it remains an untested hope rather than evidence.
insights.quote: this is a molecule that our bodies create naturally.
insights.locator: Mina of Invivyd hopes people who have not vaccinated their children

top_entities: Department of Health and Human Services
